mcqs.question: A teammate says a test suite's only value is catching regressions. What is that view missing?
options: Tests also act as executable documentation and give design feedback when code is hard to test
Tests are primarily valuable for satisfying a code coverage dashboard
Regression safety is actually a side effect, not a real benefit of testing
Tests only matter once a codebase is already in production
mcqs.explanation: Regression safety is real, but tests also document behavior in a way that can't silently go stale, and hard-to-test code is usually a signal of a design problem worth fixing. A coverage dashboard is a proxy, not the actual benefit.

mcqs.question: Why does the test pyramid put the most tests at the unit layer rather than the e2e layer, given that e2e tests give more confidence per test?
options: E2E tests are actually less reliable indicators of correctness than unit tests
Unit tests are cheap enough to run in bulk, so their total confidence across thousands of tests outweighs a handful of expensive e2e tests
Regulatory and compliance standards require a majority of tests to be unit tests
E2E tests cannot be automated, so they must be kept to a minimum
mcqs.explanation: The pyramid shape follows from multiplying confidence-per-test by how many you can afford — unit tests are cheap enough to run in bulk, so their aggregate confidence wins even though any single e2e test proves more on its own. E2E tests are fully automatable; they're just expensive.

mcqs.question: A team building a component-heavy React frontend finds their unit tests for individual components rarely catch real bugs, while wiring bugs between components are common. Which testing shape best fits this situation?
options: The classic pyramid, maximizing unit tests as the cheapest layer
The ice-cream cone, leaning on manual QA to catch wiring issues
The testing trophy, weighting a wide integration layer since that's where their real bugs live
A pyramid with no integration layer at all, going straight from unit to e2e
mcqs.explanation: The testing trophy widens the integration layer for exactly this case — frontend components are often trivial in isolation, and the bugs live in the wiring between them, which integration tests catch. The classic pyramid's assumption (unit tests are the highest-value layer) doesn't hold here.

mcqs.question: A team's CI pipeline takes 45 minutes, dominated by a large end-to-end suite, while their unit test count is small. What does this describe?
options: A healthy testing trophy shape
A well-balanced test pyramid
The ice-cream-cone anti-pattern, where most confidence sits in slow, expensive tests
A sign that the codebase has too many unit tests
mcqs.explanation: A shape dominated by slow, expensive e2e tests with few cheap unit tests underneath is the ice-cream cone — it emerges under deadline pressure and produces slow feedback loops and flaky suites, not a deliberate or balanced shape.

mcqs.question: A developer adds a test that only fails if someone breaks the test's own mock setup, never if the actual production behavior changes. What does this best illustrate?
options: A well-isolated unit test that correctly uses test doubles
Test-induced design damage — a test that increases coverage without actually catching real bugs
An integration test correctly verifying a real seam
A textbook example of executable documentation
mcqs.explanation: A test that only breaks when its own scaffolding breaks isn't testing production behavior at all — it inflates coverage numbers while giving no real regression safety, which is the core symptom of test-induced design damage rather than genuine isolation.
